# Known Vulnerabilities & Broken Candidates

Covers PQC algorithms broken during the NIST competition, implementation-level
vulnerabilities, and lessons for algorithm confidence. See
[citations.md](../citations.md) for full source details.

## Broken Algorithms

### SIKE/SIDH — Isogeny-Based Key Encapsulation (Broken August 2022)

**What happened:** Wouter Castryck and Thomas Decru published an attack that
completely broke SIDH (and thus SIKE) on August 5, 2022 [9][26]. The attack
recovered secret keys in polynomial time using a classical computer.

**Attack mechanism:** Exploited Kani's reducibility criterion for isogenies.
The auxiliary torsion point information in SIDH public keys provided enough
structure for the attack [26].

**Attack performance** [9]:
- SIKEp434: ~1 hour on a single-core PC
- SIKEp503: ~2 hours (est., from discovery agent)
- SIKEp610: ~8 hours (est., from discovery agent)
- SIKEp751: ~21 hours (est., from discovery agent)

**Caveat:** Performance times beyond SIKEp434 are from discovery agent
cross-referencing; the ePrint PDF was not directly extractable [26].

**Impact:** SIKE was immediately removed from NIST PQC Round 4 [9][30]. SIKE had
been attractive due to its small key and ciphertext sizes [2].

**Scope of damage:** Other isogeny-based systems (CGL, CSIDH, SQIsign) are
**not** based on SIDH and remain unaffected by the Castryck-Decru attack family.

### Rainbow — Multivariate Signature Scheme (Broken February 2022)

**What happened:** Ward Beullens published an attack recovering Rainbow SL1
secret keys in approximately 53 hours on a standard laptop [27].

**Attack title:** "Breaking Rainbow Takes a Weekend on a Laptop" [9][27].

**Impact:** Rainbow was excluded from final NIST selections announced July 5,
2022. CRYSTALS-Dilithium, FALCON, and SPHINCS+ were selected instead [2][28].

**Scope of damage:** Other NIST-selected algorithms are based on completely
different mathematics (lattices, hash functions), so Rainbow attack techniques
cannot transfer [2].

### GeMSS — Multivariate Signature Scheme (Not Selected)

GeMSS was not cryptographically broken via a complete key recovery attack like
Rainbow. It was dropped due to [28]:
- Public keys over 100 KB
- Slow signing times
- Partial cryptanalysis undermining parameter confidence

## Implementation Vulnerabilities

### KyberSlash — Timing Side-Channel Attacks

KyberSlash1 and KyberSlash2 target ML-KEM implementations via
secret-dependent division timing [29]:

- **Mechanism:** Division operations in decryption/encryption leak timing
  information correlated with secret key material
- **Attack performance:** ML-KEM-512 complete secret key recovery in
  approximately 10 minutes on Intel processors (est.) [29]
- **Clangover:** The Clang compiler in some versions/optimization settings
  converts constant-time source code into secret-dependent machine code,
  creating timing leaks invisible at the source code level [29]
- **Affected:** Reference implementation and several open-source libraries

**Caveat:** KyberSlash paper (PDF) was not directly extractable; details from
discovery agent [29].

### Lattice-Based Side-Channel Attacks (General)

Academic research demonstrates several attack vectors [47][48]:

- **Polynomial multiplication attacks:** Non-profiled correlation power analysis
  successfully extracts secret keys from all NIST final-round lattice-based KEMs
  by targeting Toom-Cook and NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) operations [47]

- **NTT as primary target:** The NTT is the main building block of lattice-based
  implementations and the primary target for side-channel attacks [48]. Single-trace
  attacks can recover private keys from one decryption observation [48].

- **Attack efficiency:** Advanced two-step attacks combining generic
  distinguishers and lattice reduction show 23,490× speedup over baseline
  methods [48].

- **Chosen-ciphertext side-channel:** Recent methods reduce traces needed for
  key recovery by 66.67% compared to previous approaches [48].

### Countermeasures

- **Masking:** Randomizing twiddle factors in NTT provides protection; no leakage
  observed with 1,000× more traces than unprotected versions required [48]
- **Shuffling:** Randomizing butterfly operation order within NTT stages shows
  only 8.7% hardware efficiency degradation [48]
- **Constant-time implementation:** Essential but insufficient alone due to
  compiler-level vulnerabilities (Clangover) [29]
- **Assembly-level verification:** Required to confirm constant-time behavior
  after compilation [29]
- **Machine learning resistance:** Deep learning applied to side-channel attacks
  has compromised many countermeasures; models excel at extracting features from
  raw data [48]

### Fault Injection

Fault attacks exploit fault propagation in masked implementations, typically
through Arithmetic-to-Boolean (A2B) conversion [48].

## Lessons for Algorithm Confidence

### What the Breaks Tell Us

1. **Mathematical diversity matters.** Both SIKE and Rainbow used mathematics
   (isogenies, multivariate polynomials) that proved vulnerable to unexpected
   classical attacks. NIST's decision to diversify across lattice, hash-based,
   and code-based families reflects this lesson [2].

2. **Scrutiny time correlates with confidence.** Lattice-based problems (LWE,
   NTRU) have resisted cryptanalysis for 20+ years. Hash-based security relies
   on well-understood hash function properties. Code-based problems (McEliece)
   have resisted attacks for 40+ years. SIKE's isogeny-based approach was newer
   and less studied [5][7].

3. **Implementation ≠ algorithm security.** KyberSlash and NTT side-channel
   attacks target implementations, not the mathematical hardness of the
   underlying problems. Correct algorithm selection is necessary but not
   sufficient [29][47][48].

4. **Compiler trust boundaries.** Clangover demonstrates that security
   guarantees at the source code level can be violated by compiler
   optimizations. Security-critical code requires assembly-level verification [29].

5. **Speed of cryptanalysis.** Both SIKE and Rainbow were broken within months
   of Round 3 selection (July 2022 → August 2022 for SIKE, February 2022 for
   Rainbow). The breaks came from unexpected mathematical insights, not
   incremental advances [9][27].

### Confidence Assessment of Current Standards

| Algorithm | Mathematical Basis | Scrutiny Period | Confidence |
|-----------|-------------------|-----------------|------------|
| ML-KEM/ML-DSA | Module-LWE/SIS | ~20 years (LWE introduced 2005) | High |
| SLH-DSA | Hash function security | Decades (hash-based sigs since 1970s) | Very High |
| FN-DSA | NTRU lattices | ~25 years (NTRU introduced 1998) | High |
| HQC | Code-based (quasi-cyclic) | ~10 years (HQC proposed 2017) | Moderate-High |

SLH-DSA's "very high" confidence reflects that its security relies only on
hash function preimage and collision resistance — the most conservative and
well-understood assumption among all PQC standards [8].
